name: Deload weeks / rest days

lead: A deload is a planned lighter week of training, and rest days are days without training. Lifters use them so fatigue dissipates and they can keep progressing toward a more muscular physique.

Reducing volume or intensity lets recovery catch up while fitness is retained, which supports steadier progress over months. The idea comes from periodization, a method of planning training rooted in Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome and formalised by Leo Matveyev around 1964. Direct trials of deloads are sparse and none measure appearance.

paras: Lifters typically cut volume or intensity for a week every so often, or take scheduled rest days between hard sessions. It is commonly built into a programme, with deloads triggered by accumulated fatigue or placed on a fixed calendar. Training resumes at normal loads afterward.
Overtraining from insufficient recovery is the documented concern, and it is usually treated with rest and reduced load. Deloads themselves carry no specific reported harms.

angle.text: Planned lighter weeks and rest days let fatigue clear so you can keep training hard and adding muscle. The approach follows periodization theory; direct trials of deloads are sparse and none measure appearance.

lead: Deload weeks and rest days are planned reductions in training load that lifters use to keep building muscle and strength over the long run. A deload is typically a week of reduced volume or intensity; rest days are days without training. People use them so that fatigue clears, joints and connective tissue recover, and the next block of training can be done harder, which is the chain behind more muscle, a better physique and a more athletic look.[1][2][3]

The concept sits inside periodization, a cyclical method of planning training that draws on Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome and was formalised by Leo Matveyev around 1964.[1] A related idea, supercompensation, proposed by Nikolai Yakovlev in the 1950s, holds that after training lowers fitness, recovery restores it and then lifts it above the starting level.[2] Wikipedia's periodization article does not use the word 'deload' but describes transition phases of 3-4 weeks and alternating hard and light days.[1]

In lifting communities, the deload is a routine part of training talk. T Nation members describe feeling run down and poor sleep as signs a deload was due, and discuss how diet and habits tend to slip during a deload week.[4][5][6] Overtraining, a failure to recover, is typically treated with rest and reduced load.[7]
infobox: A week of reduced volume or intensity

paras: Periodization aims to keep athletes in Selye's resistance stage so recovery raises baseline.[1] The fitness-fatigue model of Banister expresses performance as fitness minus fatigue.[1] Critics such as Kiely (2018) argue early models were oversimplified.[1]

Supercompensation describes training as temporarily lowering fitness, after which recovery returns it to baseline and then overshoots. Wikipedia notes that timing matters: a session during recovery may lead to overtraining, one during supercompensation can raise fitness further, and one after it leaves the body at baseline. Tendons and bone adapt more slowly than muscle.[2] The article describes the model as postulated and its parameters as not fully understood.[2]

sections.h: Rest days, recovery and muscle growth
paras: Wikipedia's article on muscle hypertrophy reports that muscle protein synthesis after resistance training rises and returns to normal after roughly 28 hours in adequately fed young males in one study, while another found it still elevated at 72 hours. It also lists replenishing glycogen after training as aiding recovery, and training frequency as a variable affecting hypertrophy.[3] Rest days are where lifters place this recovery.

Overtraining involves persistent fatigue, elevated resting heart rate and performance decline.[7] The page lists breaks, reduced volume or intensity, sleep and nutrition as measures, while noting limited evidence detail.[7]

On T Nation, one member writes that a bout of disrupted sleep and being run down is the sign someone should have deloaded the previous week, comparing it to excess adrenaline or cortisol from pushing hard too long.[4] Another confesses wanting a full week without training as a deload.[5] A forum user reports that during a lifting program his diet and other decisions improve, and that on a deload week he is more likely to drink, stay up late and skimp on water.[6]

On looksmax.org, rest days appear in threads about body fat and gym routines, including a poster who says he hit new strength records after two rest days, and another who finds rest days hard because gym attendance fills his schedule.[8][9]
No studies found specifically testing scheduled deload weeks in the sources reviewed. Related research on periodization and overtraining exists.[1][7]

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation and looksmax.org discuss deloads and rest days as part of training and recovery routines.[4][5][6][8][9]
